profile.summary: Tranception is an autoregressive transformer language model for protein fitness prediction, from the Marks lab and the OATML group. It scores a mutated protein sequence by how likely the model thinks that sequence is, and it can optionally blend that score with counts from an alignment of homologous sequences retrieved at inference time. It handles substitutions, multiple mutants and insertions or deletions, and it was published together with the ProteinGym benchmark.

summary_quotes.text: We introduce Tranception, a novel transformer architecture leveraging autoregressive predictions and retrieval of homologous sequences at inference to achieve state-of-the-art fitness prediction performance.
Given its markedly higher performance on multiple mutants, robustness to shallow alignments and ability to score indels, our approach offers significant gain of scope over existing approaches.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tranception is a decoder-only transformer built on two ideas: making attention heads specialise, and reading patterns from contiguous subsequences. In each layer the attention heads are split into four groups; three of them apply depthwise convolutions with kernel sizes 3, 5 and 7 after the query, key and value projections, so each group mixes information over a different range. The published configuration uses a squared-relu activation, grouped ALiBi position embeddings and a 25-token vocabulary. The model was trained to predict the next residue on UniRef100, with half of the sequences reversed at random; the paper scores each sequence in both directions and averages the two log-likelihood ratios. At inference the model's own autoregressive log-likelihood can be combined with weighted pseudocounts computed at each alignment position, using the sequence weighting procedure of Hopf et al. with the default thresholds. The configuration file carries the retrieval weight for that blend; the paper selected 0.6. Scoring insertions and deletions with retrieval also needs Clustal Omega, because the mutated sequence has to be realigned.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are published: Small, Medium and Large, downloadable as zip archives from the Marks lab server (about 400MB, 1.4GB and 3.1GB unzipped) and also on the Hugging Face hub. They differ in depth and width: 12 layers and width 768 (Small, 85M parameters), 24 and 1024 (Medium, 300M) and 36 and 1280 (Large, 700M), with parameter counts as the paper gives them. All three use a context of 1024 positions. A result must say which checkpoint was used and whether retrieval was on (the --inference_time_retrieval flag), and with retrieval it must also name the alignment and the weights file. This page read the Hugging Face revisions d1ef6271 (Large), 96f42978 (Medium) and 303ff126 (Small).

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Autoregressive transformer protein language model for fitness prediction, with optional retrieval of homologous sequences at inference.

quotes.text: a novel transformer architecture leveraging autoregressive predictions and retrieval of homologous sequences at inference
Tranception is a novel autoregressive transformer architecture

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Decoder-only transformer with grouped ALiBi position embeddings, a squared-relu activation, and attention heads split into four groups, three of which apply depthwise convolutions of kernel size 3, 5 or 7. Large: 36 layers, width 1280, 20 heads, inner size 5120. Medium: 24 layers, width 1024, 16 heads. Small: 12 layers, width 768, 12 heads. Vocabulary of 25 tokens.
facts.source_locator: config.json files; paper: Figure 1 legend and Table 5

quotes.text: Attention heads at each layer are split into 4 distinct groups.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A protein sequence and the mutants to score, given as a deep mutational scanning file referenced from a reference CSV. With retrieval, also an alignment folder and a sequence weights folder for the protein.

quotes.text: The MSAs used to train alignment-based methods or used at inference in Tranception with retrieval

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Fitness scores for the mutated sequences, written to an output scores folder. A separate script compares those scores with ground truth labels using Spearman's rank correlation, AUC and MCC.
facts.source_locator: examples script; README: Fitness prediction with Tranception

quotes.text: across the different metrics discussed in the paper (ie., Spearman's rank correlation, AUC, MCC)

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: 85M (Small), 300M (Medium) and 700M (Large), as the paper's Table 5 gives them. No exact counts are published; the Hugging Face API gives none because the weights are stored as pytorch_model.bin.

quotes.text: Our largest transformer model, Tranception L, has 700M parameters and is trained on UniRef100

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: UniRef100, after mild filtering: about 249 million sequences for training and 2.5 million held out for validation. Singletons at the UniRef50 cluster level, sequences with pyrrolysine or selenocysteine, and sequences with two or more consecutive X were removed. Ablations on UniRef90 and UniRef50 did worse, so the larger models were trained on UniRef100.

quotes.text: We use 99% of the data (∼ 249 million sequences) for training and set aside 1% of the data for validation (∼ 2.5 million sequences).
All singletons at the UniRef50 cluster level are removed
but observed superior performance from training on UniRef100

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: Three checkpoints: Tranception Small, Tranception Medium and Tranception Large, each on the Marks lab server and the Hugging Face hub. Retrieval is an inference setting switched on by --inference_time_retrieval, not a separate checkpoint.

facts.value: Not stated. The paper trains on UniRef100 but does not give the release or download date. The alignments it built for ProteinGym retrieval used UniRef100 downloaded on 24 November 2021. The paper is in the proceedings of ICML 2022 and was posted to arXiv on 27 May 2022.

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: 1024 positions (n_ctx and n_positions) in all three checkpoint configurations; the paper chose 1,024 tokens because it covers about 98% of UniRef100 sequences. Longer proteins are scored through a window chosen to keep as much context as possible around the mutation, which the configuration sets as optimal.

quotes.text: as it allows to handle 98% of protein sequences in UniRef100 without truncation.
For single mutations, the optimal scoring window is selected so as to maximize the context available around that mutation

strengths.text: Scores insertions and deletions as well as substitutions and multiple mutants, which the authors describe as a gain in scope over existing approaches.
strengths.source_locator: README: Abstract, Fitness prediction with Tranception

quotes.text: To predict the fitness of mutated sequences (substitutions and indels) with Tranception
ability to score indels, our approach offers significant gain of scope over existing approaches

strengths.text: Retrieval is optional, so the same checkpoint can be used where no alignment is available and the authors report robustness to shallow alignments.
Code and checkpoints are MIT licensed, and the alignments, sequence weights and published score files are all downloadable.

limitations.text: Context is 1024 positions, so longer proteins are handled through a scoring window rather than in one pass.
Retrieval needs an alignment and per-sequence weights for the protein, and scoring indels with retrieval also needs Clustal Omega installed.

To compute sequence weights for new proteins, you may use the MSA_processing class under `tranception/utils/msa_utils.py`.

limitations.text: The environment is pinned to python 3.8, pytorch 1.9.1 with cudatoolkit 10.2 and transformers 4.17, and the repository was last pushed in 2023.
The authors note that their larger networks still appear undertrained after 150k training steps.

run_guide.summary: Set up the repository at a pinned commit, download the Tranception Large checkpoint and the ProteinGym alignments and weights, and score a deep mutational scanning assay with retrieval.
prerequisites: conda, to build the environment from tranception_env.yml. It pins python 3.8, pytorch 1.9.1, cudatoolkit 10.2 and transformers 4.17.
Clustal Omega, if retrieval is used when scoring insertions and deletions.
Disk space: about 3.1GB for the Large checkpoint unzipped, about 2.2GB for the ProteinGym alignments and about 68M for the weights. The code and checkpoints are MIT licensed and not gated.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/OATML-Markslab/Tranception.git
cd Tranception
git checkout --detach 2ddf40e1db9d2d180d1b5fc9d1b39ad5b04fbb6d
steps.explanation: The README's clone line, with cd and checkout added to get the repository at the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda env create -f tranception_env.yml
conda activate tranception_env
steps.explanation: The README's environment step. The activate line is added; the environment name comes from tranception_env.yml.

steps.title: Download the checkpoint
steps.shell:
curl -o Tranception_Large_checkpoint.zip https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/tranception/Tranception_Large_checkpoint.zip
unzip Tranception_Large_checkpoint.zip
rm Tranception_Large_checkpoint.zip
steps.explanation: The README's download step for Tranception Large, unchanged. The Medium and Small archives are on the same server, and the same checkpoints are on the Hugging Face hub.

steps.title: Download the alignments and sequence weights
steps.shell:
curl -o MSA_ProteinGym.zip https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/tranception/MSA_ProteinGym.zip
unzip MSA_ProteinGym.zip
rm MSA_ProteinGym.zip
curl -o MSA_weights.zip https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/tranception/MSA_weights.zip
unzip MSA_weights.zip
rm MSA_weights.zip
steps.explanation: The README's two download steps, needed only for scoring with retrieval. The weights were computed with the Hopf et al. procedure at the default thresholds.

steps.title: Score one assay with retrieval
steps.shell:
cd examples
export checkpoint=$PATH_TO_MODEL_CHECKPOINT
export DMS_data_folder=$PATH_TO_DMS_SUBSTITUTIONS
export DMS_index=$INDEX_OF_DMS_TO_BE_SCORED_IN_REFERENCE_FILE
export output_scores_folder=$PATH_TO_OUTPUT_SCORES
export MSA_folder=$PATH_TO_MSA
export MSA_weights_folder=$PATH_TO_MSA_WEIGHTS_SUBSTITUTIONS
export DMS_reference_file_path="../proteingym/ProteinGym_reference_file_substitutions.csv"
python3 ../score_tranception_proteingym.py \
                --checkpoint ${checkpoint} \
                --DMS_reference_file_path ${DMS_reference_file_path} \
                --DMS_data_folder ${DMS_data_folder} \
                --DMS_index ${DMS_index} \
                --output_scores_folder ${output_scores_folder} \
                --inference_time_retrieval \
                --MSA_folder ${MSA_folder} \
                --MSA_weights_folder ${MSA_weights_folder}
steps.explanation: The repository's own example script, with a cd line added because it uses paths relative to the examples folder. The six placeholder paths must be filled in with the folders downloaded above; the script's own comment says to replace them.

The [examples](https://github.com/OATML-Markslab/Tranception/tree/main/examples) folder provides several bash scripts illustrating how these two scripts may be used.

outputs: Fitness scores for the chosen assay's mutants in the output scores folder. The performance analysis script then reports Spearman's rank correlation, AUC and MCC against the assay labels; the sources read do not show the file names.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The scoring script expects the ProteinGym file layout and a reference CSV, so it is not a single-sequence API.
The pinned environment (python 3.8, pytorch 1.9.1, cudatoolkit 10.2) is from 2022 and may not install on current hardware.
Clustal Omega is needed for retrieval on indels and is not installed by these steps.
